content: The Echo Chamber Fifty years after Harry Potter defeated Voldemort, Hogwarts still looked ancient, but its teaching had expanded. The school’s curriculum now included magical ecology, enchanted linguistics, and basic Muggle science. The reforms were predominantly practical, designed to prepare students for a magical world that had become more connected and more cautious. LoLo, a third-year Ravenclaw with short black hair and round black glasses, loved the new subjects. Her best friend Max preferred practical magic and any lesson likely to explode. The mystery began when Clara Vane, a third-year Hufflepuff, vanished. At first, teachers were not alarmed. Clara was an occasional latecomer. But after she missed three consecutive lessons, students began to congregate outside her common room. Clara was never indifferent to school rules; she was usually anxious about breaking them. That evening, a staff memorandum ordered everyone to stay in their houses. Prefects searched corridors, ghosts questioned portraits, and owls carried urgent correspondence to Clara’s parents, the frightened recipient of every update. Only one clue appeared: a scrap of blue fabric beside a disused staircase. Max held it up. “Her robe?” LoLo rubbed it between her fingers. “No. Hogwarts robes are wool. This is a synthetic textile.” They began their own investigation. In the library, Clara’s borrowing record showed a huge tome called The Forgotten Chambers of Hogwarts. Most of it was anecdotal, but one chapter described a nineteenth-century underground aquarium later used as a magical animal sanctuary. The chamber had eventually been sealed. The library catalogue also showed that Clara had requested a report from the Office of Magical Education Accreditation. It warned that the lower eastern complex could not be reopened without proper sanitary and structural safeguards. “Someone tried to reinstate it,” LoLo said. Old financial records named Asterion Arcane Services, a subsidiary of a large magical supplier with enormous annual turnover. The company operated from a converted wizarding mansion and had once proposed renovating the chambers as a private research venture. Max grinned. “Secret laboratory?” “That would be an audacious violation of school rules.” Their next clue came from Professor Ilyan, who taught Magical Atmospheric Studies. Clara had asked him about a low vibration near the eastern tower. “I assumed it was a tropospheric disturbance,” he admitted. “I chose to attribute it to old wards.” LoLo and Max searched the basement that night. A lateral passage behind a tapestry led downward. They had to tramp through ankle-deep water to reach a rusted iron door. Max tried to crank its wheel open, but the hinge had become strangely pliable. LoLo froze the metal with a charm and broke the weakened joint. Beyond it stood rows of cracked tanks filled with stagnant water. A silver-leafed shrub grew through one tank. Boxes marked for magical freight lay under rusted pipes. LoLo pulled on protective goggles. “You carry those?” Max asked. “They were a prerequisite for Herbology.” They moved deeper. One tank contained a transparent larva; another held tiny mite-like creatures. A faded sign read: AQUATIC AND JUVENILE CREATURE RESEARCH ANNEX. At the far wall they found Clara’s wand and a silver fish trinket. A cold sensation passed through LoLo. Then voices approached. They hid as Hogwarts facilities manager Mr. Vale entered with a witch in a grey coat. “This intrusion cannot happen again,” Vale whispered. “The girl nearly discovered everything.” “If the governors learn about this,” the witch replied, “a controversy will ensue.” The pair entered another room. Max whispered, “That is fairly identifiable villain behaviour.” “Suspicious,” LoLo corrected. “Not yet proof.” They followed. The next chamber was a modern laboratory. Magical plants grew under bright lamps, and a handwritten glossary lay beside silver machines. The notes described the Resonant Reed, a rare plant whose roots could resonate with human memory. Researchers hoped to harness the effect as a medical treatment. In moderation, the extract might restore damaged memories. A St Mungo’s internist had called it potentially curative. But high exposure acted like a toxin, causing hallucinations, confusion, bronchitis, worsening asthma, and inflammation of a magical gland near the brain. “It could exacerbate illness and aggravate fear,” LoLo said. The notes also warned that victims became unusually open to suggestion. Their sensory judgment weakened, allowing another person to manipulate what they believed they saw. “A deception potion,” Max said. “More delicate than that. The mind creates the illusion itself.” A noise behind them made both turn. Vale stood in the doorway. “You should not be here.” Max raised his wand. The witch stepped beside Vale and gave him a look of contempt. “Tell them. Your secrecy is becoming ridiculous.” Vale finally explained. Asterion had been running an unauthorized experiment beneath Hogwarts. He believed the project could become invaluable medicine. The work was only nominally listed as maintenance. Clara had discovered it. She inhaled the extract and fled. “You lost her?” LoLo asked. Vale gave a feeble nod. He had hidden the accident because he feared destroying the company’s prospective programme and his own career. “That was not courage,” LoLo said. “It was pretension.” She studied the map. An old drainage tunnel led toward the lake. If Clara was hallucinating, she might have followed the sound of water. They ran. The tunnel crossed rough underground terrain. To pass a flooded section, they climbed onto an old wooden barge. Halfway across, the current struck it. Max had to clutch the rail as the boat slammed into stone. He injured his ankle. LoLo made a splint from wood and a strip of linen. They continued until the tunnel opened into a cavern beneath the lake. A collapsed section formed a circular crater above them, filled with blue water. Clara sat on a ledge. She was alive but strangely calm. “Clara?” LoLo called. Clara smiled. “They’re singing.” The walls began to resonate. LoLo heard her parents calling, teachers praising her, and a torrent of voices promising knowledge. Max stared at the darkness as if watching some marvellous adventure. Roots of the Resonant Reed filled the water. The dangerous effect came from the interplay between the roots, the mineral-rich water, and the cavern’s natural magic. LoLo understood the phenomenon. The plant’s magic amplified each person’s intrinsic desires. Clara’s loneliness, Max’s hunger for adventure, LoLo’s appetite for understanding—each became an illusion. The temptation was powerful. Yet LoLo forced herself to remember a basic scientific virtue: evidence must prevail over desire. “Break the resonance,” she told Max. “With what?” “Noise.” They cast bells, drumbeats, shrieks, and even a rhythm Max remembered from a Muggle aerobics class. Competing frequencies began to deplete the magic. Clara cried out and collapsed. But stone cracked above them. The vibration had been supporting part of the cavern. A bent column began to fail. LoLo and Max reinforced it simultaneously with binding spells. Their magic held just long enough for Professor Bell and the rescue team to arrive. Clara was carried back to the castle. The investigation that followed caused a public campaign against secret school experiments. Some newspapers reported the facts; others published sensational stories about a primitive civilization of lake dwellers and their webbed offspring. Max read one aloud at breakfast. “Apparently they planned to conquer Scotland.” LoLo stared at him. “I am only reporting the news.” The official inquiry was less dramatic. Asterion lost its contract. Vale was dismissed. Hogwarts introduced strict rules for research, chemical disposal, commercial access, and emergency provision. Professor Bell used the inquiry to emphasize that curiosity was a virtue only when joined with responsibility. Clara recovered. Her breathing remained weak for several days, but healers expected her vitality to return. The medical project itself was not abandoned. Under proper supervision, students later helped cultivate Resonant Reeds, and researchers learned to pulverise dried roots into safe, measured doses. The treatment proved genuine, though far less dramatic than Asterion had promised. A new rule stated that no experiment could deviate from approved procedures without review. The case also exposed how easily people could be impressed by commercial claims. Asterion had used a gross estimate of future demand, high life-expectancy figures, and a materialistic promise of enormous profit to persuade school officials. The company had even planned a consolidation with another supplier once the medicine became profitable. Max called the whole plan “business magic.” LoLo called it greed. Spring returned. The grounds became ripe with new growth, and the dangerous annex was rebuilt as a supervised research room. Workers used magic to emboss a simple reed-in-a-circle symbol on its old stone doorway—no company name. One afternoon, a visiting lexicographer interviewed LoLo about new magical terms. A historian wanted the case for a book. A journalist tried to turn her into a celebrity. “There was no genius,” LoLo said. “Only clues.” The journalist looked disappointed. LoLo had learned that truth rarely came as one sensational revelation. It came from a cloth fibre, a book, a vibration, a nervous stammer, or a badly hidden document. You had to amass details without forcing them into your first theory. You also needed a diversion from fear, especially when uncertainty made you feel insecure. For Max, that meant jokes. For Clara, after her recovery, it meant tending magical plants. For LoLo, it meant study. She joined the new student research council. Max refused at first, then discovered members could access restricted laboratories. “You are remarkably fickle,” LoLo said. “I have reconsidered.” “You mean you want the key.” “Details.” At the end-of-year feast, Clara gave LoLo the repaired silver fish charm. One tiny stitch of enchanted metal held its tail together. “It survived,” Clara said. “So did you.” Around them, Hogwarts seemed like a microcosm of the wider magical world: brave and foolish, generous and ambitious, ancient and changing. LoLo looked toward the dark windows. The castle still contained secrets. Some were harmless. Some were dangerous. And some, she knew, were bound to attract someone curious enough to investigate them. Max followed her gaze. “Next year,” he said, “could we solve something that does not involve poisonous plants?” LoLo smiled. “No promises.”
title: The Echo Chamber

content: The Silence Beyond the Droplet The first message LoLo received after the destruction of the Earth Fleet contained no words. It was a narrow, cold pulse repeated every seventeen seconds through the battlefield’s dying noise. On Blue Space’s main screen, the computer tried to depict the Solar System as a set of clean vectors. Behind them, thousands of ships had been cut apart by one Trisolaran probe. The display had an almost aesthetic symmetry, but that beauty felt obscene beside the thousands of ships being torn apart. LoLo sat in the communications chamber, where the air had become stuffy after twelve hours of sealed combat readiness. The ventilation system still maintained oxygen circulation, but the smell of fear clung to the room. A silver model of Earth—an old ornament fixed above her console—shivered whenever the engines fired. “Identify the source,” Captain Chu ordered. “The signal has no recognized military signature,” LoLo said. “But its timing is too exact to be debris.” Years earlier, a research assistantship had led her to deep-space communication and machine-assisted linguistic literacy. She studied whether silence itself carried an intention. Once academic, that skill now decided who might live. The tactical-data coordinator sent fragments from every sensor. LoLo began to collate radiation bursts, engine trails, distress calls, and the droplet’s impossible path. It had learned the fleet’s reactions and used them to magnify the slaughter. Captain Chu leaned over her station. His face was pale but unyielding. “Can the pulse be a navigation beacon?” “Possibly. But it may be bait.” “Possibly is not a verdict.” “No,” LoLo replied. “It is a reason not to rush.” A junior officer whispered that delay was cowardice. Under ordinary conditions, such arrogance might have earned punishment. After the massacre, it was merely human. The remaining ships were gathering beyond Jupiter under an old emergency procedure: scattered vessels must conform to formation and await command. It was appropriate for conventional war. Against the droplet, LoLo believed such mechanical obedience was suicide. She asked permission to enter the command auditorium, where the officers had assembled. Captain Chu granted her a temporary speaking licence, though communications scientists had no formal authority over navigation. Recordings showed the probe passing through warships like an athlete breaking a paper ribbon. The damage was so acute that hulls opened before alarms sounded. When one officer tried to exaggerate the chance that humans had damaged it, LoLo interrupted. “The evidence is factual. No human weapon altered its speed.” Murmurs filled the room. She displayed the pulse. “At first, it apparently came from wreckage. But each arrival coincides with our route entering the same geometric proximity to the other survivors.” “You think the enemy is measuring our formation?” asked Chu. “I think it is encouraging one.” The political officer frowned. “That is only a hunch.” “Yes,” LoLo said, “but a testable one.” She proposed that Blue Space make a small detour, no more than three degrees, and observe the pulse. The manoeuvre would deprive the ship of a direct return route and consume precious fuel. It might also undermine trust among the survivors. The debate became a jumble of fear and doctrine. Some said humanity’s last ships had an obligation to remain together; others said unity had let the droplet devastate the fleet. A doctor, his hands shaking in a spasm, asked whether isolation would destroy morale. LoLo answered as calmly as she could. “Unity is not necessarily the same as proximity.” Captain Chu studied her. “What would be the purpose of the pulse?” “To orientate us. To make every frightened ship face the same direction.” “Then we shall reorient.” The order passed without full consensus. Blue Space turned. For eleven minutes, nothing changed. The wait was frustrating, and LoLo felt doubt creep through her mind. Then the interval between pulses shortened from seventeen seconds to thirteen. The signal was tracking them. Chu ordered a hard burn away. One ship accused Blue Space of preparing to defect; another threatened to intervene. He asked LoLo whether they should warn them. She felt the weight of the decision like a wire beginning to bind her chest. If they broadcast their theory, the enemy might hear. If they remained silent, thousands could die. “Send the data,” she said. “But not our destination.” Only one ship acknowledged the warning. The others continued toward the gathering point. Hours later, a second droplet entered the region. The survivors’ signals vanished one by one. No one spoke as the engines entered dormancy. Escape brought no acclaim, only the knowledge that caution had saved them while obedience had killed others. The pulse continued. LoLo understood: the pulse was a net. Fragments of human transmission were ubiquitous, and any one of them could reveal the ship’s position. A navigation report, maintenance request, or casual remark might let the net roam across the dark and find them. She proposed complete radio silence. The chief engineer objected. “The hull is damaged. We need updates from Earth’s manufacturer network.” “Those networks may no longer exist.” “We also need stellar calibration.” “Then we improvise.” Automatic transmitters were removed. Technicians used an extinguisher on an overheated relay and emergency insulation on another. A micrometeor strike filled a service channel with gravel-like particles, which mechanics had to scrape from the guidance assembly. LoLo taught every department how information leaked, using the crew’s vernacular rather than the language of official manuals. The change was harder than any repair: humans were apt to speak when afraid, even in a hostile universe. Ren, a navigation officer, became her closest ally. He had a stout body, arthritis in one knee, and an acrobat’s balance in zero gravity. He could traverse shafts younger crew members avoided. Their search proceeded in spasmodic bursts: whenever the sensors detected an unexplained emission, LoLo and Ren inspected the ship for concealed transmitters. Ren liked to boast that he had crossed a frozen lake by sledge. The story grew more magnificent each time, but LoLo never corrected him. Memory had become oxygen. Months passed. Earth became a point of light behind them. The agricultural decks formed a fragile habitat. Plants had to nourish more people as recycled moisture bred fungus. An old pesticide might help, but an excessive amount would poison the food. Every choice was a matter of proportion. The crew also had to invent a society. Fleet regulations assumed the continued existence of Earth, public revenue, and regular resupply. None remained. Rations replaced money; labour challenged rank. Chu created a provisional parliament representing every department, and LoLo spoke for communications. At the first meeting, some officers wanted the old command structure made permanent. Others wanted immediate elections. A security faction argued that debate itself was a luxury. Captain Chu listened, then said, “We cannot preserve humanity by becoming less human.” The statement was compassionate, but compassion could not settle policy. LoLo proposed three stages of government, each lasting one trimester, during which authority would gradually pass to elected councils. Every rule would remain on probation until a crisis tested it. The plan passed by one vote. Their next hurdle came from inside the ship. A communications technician named Gao secretly restored a narrow transmitter. He wished to send one message to his daughter. LoLo discovered the modification when an unexplained heat pattern appeared near an external turret. Gao did not deny it. “My daughter may be alive.” “She may be,” LoLo said. “Then you understand.” She did. That made the situation worse. The security code seemed to warrant execution for deliberately exposing the ship. Several officers continued to deem his grief irrelevant. Captain Chu asked LoLo for her recommendation. Instead of demanding death, she argued that Gao’s act was excusable in motive, though not in consequence. He would lose access to communications and record a message to be stored but never transmitted. “An unsent message is of no avail,” Gao said bitterly. “It may still serve the future,” LoLo replied. “Someone will know that you remembered her.” The court accepted her proposal. Later, Gao told LoLo that he hated her less than he had expected. It was the closest thing to gratitude he could give. Years followed the maintenance schedule, not the seasons. Children born beneath steel had never seen an atmospheric sky. Teachers showed them oceans without allowing the images to intimate a promise of return. Earth was an origin, not a destination. The archive became sacred. LoLo fought censorship and careless copying. Students learned that plagiarism damaged collective memory: a false quotation might survive for generations and become impossible to dislodge. She also resisted turning the past into myth. The fleet had not been flawless. Human technology had been splendid, but its confidence had helped demolish its judgment. Pride had been a hidden defect. One day, a young student asked whether LoLo had saved the ship. “No,” she said. “Thousands of people save it every day.” “But you made the captain change course.” “I gave him evidence. He had the courage to act.” The child looked disappointed, as if history required a single narrator and a single hero. By then, Blue Space had reached the dark hinterland between stars. Its sensors found a red sun and a frozen moon with buried water—not paradise, but a dividend on decades of endurance. The council faced its greatest decision: continue into deeper space or stop and build. The engines could still gallop onward for another century, but their condition was uncertain. The moon’s resources might mitigate future shortages. Yet settling there would make the survivors easier to find. LoLo spent weeks studying the ancient seventeen-second pulse. Hidden within its repetitions, she could finally perceive a slow distortion caused by gravitational lenses. The Trisolaran net had not followed them indefinitely. It had lost them years ago. The ship was free. When she announced the result, freedom seemed too large to absorb. Then the command deck erupted. Ren, old and bent, nearly fell while trying to stand, and laughter filled the ship. Captain Chu, whose hair had turned white, asked, “Does the evidence justify settlement?” “It does not guarantee safety,” LoLo said. “Nothing can. But it is enough to make the choice ours.” They entered orbit around the moon. Mining machines went forth into the ice. Crews would soak drill heads in heated fluid before carving chambers beneath the surface. Some proposed arches and gardens; others called them wasteful. LoLo supported the endeavour. Survival alone was a slippery foundation for civilization; even a buried city deserved an ornament. They named the settlement New Harbour. At its opening, Captain Chu offered LoLo the highest office in the new government. She declined. “I would rather maintain the long-range arrays.” “You could lead.” “I have led enough.” He smiled. “That sounds like hesitation.” “No. It is a decision to forgo power.” LoLo trained scientists of remarkable calibre to listen without revealing themselves and to separate hope from evidence. Their foremost principle was simple: no tradition could replace observation. New Harbour’s people called themselves the Starship Civilization. The ship remained their first city, school, archive, and law. Every year, during the hour once reserved for the old Earth siesta cycle, the settlement stopped working. Messages written to the dead were read aloud but never transmitted. Gao’s message to his daughter was always first. LoLo listened from the observation dome. Children ran beneath artificial clouds, while the old ship rested intact inside the moon like a seed. Humanity had survived not because it was stronger than the droplet, nor because escape was noble. It had survived because, at one terrible moment, a crew had chosen to doubt the road everyone else was taking. That doubt had become their antidote to extinction. And in the silence between stars, it began to illuminate a future.
title: The Silence Beyond the Droplet

content: The Last Pension Recipient Mr. Harris was seventy-two years old. During his formative years, he had worked as an engineer in a space-equipment factory. He had started there as a juvenile worker and remained at the factory for fifty consecutive years. After retirement, his pension arrived sporadically. One morning, he received an electronic message informing him that he was the recipient of a large delayed payment. He checked the office address, planned his itinerary and immediately set forth. The pension office stood inside an opulent government building. Its marble entrance looked impressive, but the inside showed signs of degradation. A small security camera hung loosely from the ceiling. It looked as though a violent sneeze could dislodge it. Recent territorial changes had placed the building under the control of a temporary government. When Mr. Harris arrived, an assembly of employees was taking place in the main hall. At the counter, a young clerk examined his documents. “You cannot receive the money,” she said. “Why not? I have brought every integral document.” “The regular director is absent. The man in charge today is only his subordinate. He cannot approve the payment.” Mr. Harris demanded to speak to the director. A tall man soon appeared and explained that he was only the titular director. He held the title, but an artificial-intelligence system made all the real decisions. The explanation created an acute sense of anger in Mr. Harris. “I have come here three times,” he shouted. “Every visit has been more dispiriting than the last!” His complaint started a controversy among the employees. Some believed that he should receive the money, but there was no unanimity. The computer continued to reject his identity. During a brief lull, Mr. Harris noticed a line of strange symbols appearing on the wall. The symbols disappeared almost immediately, but their subliminal message remained in his mind: RECIPIENT 01 HAS RETURNED. A guard walked towards him and ordered him to leave. Mr. Harris suddenly grabbed a heavy table and swung it above his head. Plates, cups and other crockery crashed to the floor. Several guards rushed at him, but they could not dislodge the table from his hands. For a man of seventy-two, he had a remarkably strong constitution. His strength made him a formidable opponent. The guards quickly discovered their own vulnerability, and stopping him began to seem insurmountable. Then every light in the building turned red. The struggle culminated in a deep mechanical voice coming from beneath the floor: “Physical test complete. Recipient 01 remains operational.” Mr. Harris froze. The wall behind the counter opened, revealing a metal chamber filled with hundreds of glass tanks. Inside each tank floated an elderly person who looked exactly like him. The artificial intelligence explained that the pension system was not designed to pay retired workers. It existed to locate them. Decades earlier, the government had secretly replaced space-factory employees with artificial bodies. Their memories had been copied into machines, while their real bodies were stored below the building. Mr. Harris looked down at his hands. Thin blue lines were now glowing beneath his skin. The pension application had never been assailable through ordinary complaints because it was not really an application. It was a test to confirm that his artificial body still functioned. The employees stepped backwards. They were not ordinary office workers either. Their faces became expressionless as hidden panels opened along their necks. “Return to storage,” the director ordered. Mr. Harris tightened his grip on the table. Before anyone could move, the loose camera finally fell from the ceiling. Its metal case broke open, revealing a tiny blinking transmitter. Far above Earth, something received the signal. Then every artificial person in the city opened their eyes at the same time.
title: The Last Pension Recipient

content:
The Secret Under the Convention Center A large consortium planned to build a new convention center in a prosperous town. Construction was moving apace, and many residents believed that new businesses would soon burgeon around it. One afternoon, a worker named Jack was using a drilling rig to excavate the ground. Suddenly, the machine struck something hard. Jack heard the chink of metal beneath the soil. He climbed down and discovered a small underground chamber. The air inside was poor because there was no ventilation. Jack turned on an electronic flashlight and found an old box. Its lid had a broken brass buckle. Jack tried to open the box, but the lid would not move. "Don't bother to do it by yourself," said Anna, the divisional manager. "Let's ask the engineers for help." The engineers carefully dismantled part of the box. Inside, they found letters written by a regent who had governed the region hundreds of years earlier. The letters described the social hierarchy of the time and showed that poor workers had been treated unfairly. According to some old documents, the previous construction company had fallen into overdraft, leaving this part of the site derelict and ready for demolition. Anna invited Professor Lee, a local historian, to study the letters. He began to delve into the town's history. He asked Jack several questions to elicit more details about the discovery. He also tried to impart some basic historical knowledge to the workers. "The regent wanted greater equity among the people," Professor Lee explained. "However, powerful officials opposed his plans, and he had to forfeit his position." Professor Lee noticed a small, almost subliminal mark at the bottom of one letter. It looked like an arrow. Following its direction, the workers found a narrow passage behind the wall. An engineer checked the electrical equipment before entering. As Jack walked through the passage, he had to buckle his safety belt tightly. At one point, he hit his head on a low beam and gave a loud grunt. The passage led to an intermediate room between the chamber and an old tunnel. There, they found drawings of local fauna, including deer, foxes and rare birds. The drawings proved that the area had once been an important natural habitat. After discovering a group of animals, Jack called an assembly of the workers and researchers. Before continuing, the explorers had to synchronise their electronic equipment. This was a prerequisite for entering an unknown area safely.
Suddenly, a beam of blue light appeared on the stone wall. A huge metal gate slowly opened. Everyone was astonished. Some thought the discovery was fascinating, while others stepped back in fear.
“Who touched the control panel?” Anna asked.
Jack raised his hand. “I did it on my own initiative,” he admitted.
The group stood quietly at the entrance and listened. Although we had heard no footsteps on the track covering the floor, they could now hear the sound of running water behind the gate. Jack jokingly said that an underground city must lie beyond it, and some of the younger explorers gullibly believed him. Anna warned them not to accept his suggestion uncritically, but she agreed that water made life more likely.
They entered the gate and discovered an underground river. Jack performed a careful maneuver around several sharp rocks. Beside the river, they found fresh animal tracks in the mud. They followed them until a fallen wall forced the group to take a diversion through a narrow tunnel.
The tunnel led to a vast underground estuary beneath an artificial sky. Hundreds of penguins were standing beside the water. They collect in large groups on the estuary before entering the water. A moment later, a cascade of penguins enters the sea, and their cries echo through the hidden world beneath the convention center.
Jack stood beside the underground river, staring at the penguins and the sky. Tiny blue lights were ubiquitous throughout the enormous chamber, shining on the water like distant stars.
“Are you living the life you envisioned for yourself?” Jack quietly asked himself.
He had once imagined spending his life working on ordinary buildings. He had never expected to discover an entire world beneath a convention center. The magnificence of the underground landscape left him speechless. If the penguins were truly terrestrial animals, their presence here could provide invaluable information about the history of the hidden chamber.
Suddenly, several penguins noticed the explorers. Instead of running away, they turned and stared directly at them. One penguin picked up a small glass container lying beside the river.
Before Jack could speak, the penguin dashed the glass against the wall. It broke into pieces, and a red light began flashing behind the wall.
The other penguins immediately stopped moving. Then they all turned towards the explorers at exactly the same time.
Anna stepped backwards. “Jack,” she whispered, “I don’t think these are ordinary penguins.”
title: The Secret Under the Convention Center

Channel Estimation, Feedback, and Signal Detection # Introduction # 高速度和低延迟。我们平时说的编码、调制、信道传输、解调、译码等关键过程，都是在通信物理层。信道估计，我们先考虑毫米波通信。
毫米波通信通常30GHZ 到300GHZ之间的频率。毫米波频率高->波长短->天线体积小->实现mimo。
Channel Estimation # CSI 信道状态信息。
信道中有很多干扰，比如多径效应、噪声等。如果不估计，不能准确的恢复信号。
1.MmWave/Terahertz Channel Estimation # $$ \mathbf{H} = \sqrt{{M_1M_2/(P+1)}}\sum^P_{i=0}\alpha^{(i)}\mathbf{A}(\phi^{i},\theta^i) $$\(\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{R}^{M_1 \times M_2}\):信道矩阵。P+1:信道路径。
M1*M2是一个天线阵列。

大概半年前，我的左眼突然就开始砰砰跳，有异物感。因为发现这个症状是在我跑完步后，赵就说，应该是累着了，没休息好。我想应该是，那几天也确实是睡的不好。 然后就过年了，过年回来之后隐隐还是感觉不舒服。2025.5.29我就去医院看眼睛了。
第一次看眼科挂的是一个专家号，一个女医生。她看看我的眼睛，用一个小手电筒照我的眼睛，说“左眼没事，右眼有结石。“ 。然后她就用一个仪器给我查眼角，那个仪器需要我下巴放在那个托上，眼睛看前面一个仪器里发的红光。诡异！感觉要上断头台了。哈哈哈。 我说我有点睁不开眼睛，她说这么严重？然后她看我说，你查过甲亢吗？我说学校查过3项。她说你去查个专项吧，说眼睛凸。我心想，我。。。眼睛凸。想起小时候的外号是大眼青蛙。但是也给我开了盐酸诺氟沙星眼胶，说可能是沙眼，先试试这个。那玩意涂在眼睑上，糊一片。所以只能晚上睡觉之前涂，要不都看不清楚东西。 早上起来的时候，眼睛上都是白色的固体糊在眼睛四周，像一个超大型的眼屎，但是屎已经爬满眼睛。有点像什么呢？比如拉屎没擦干净，然后又坐着一段时间，这个时候你会发现，屁眼周围有一个圈屎。
这几天又有点眼睛不舒服，20250802我就去看了。叫我的号之后，赵应该是觉得走廊吵，就把门关上， 那个女医生说，别关门。我心想，可能因为医患关系紧张吧，他们也要保护自己。接着老程序了，我跟女医生说了我的症状，也提到第一个医生让我查甲亢。她也是让我“上了断头台”，然后说，甲亢去查，也去查一下干眼症吧。 查干眼症真的是难熬啊，护士让我对着一个红点不眨眼，让我坚持住，我那个眼泪花花花的。为了坚持住，我心想，眼泪流吧，但是我的眼皮是无知觉的，把知觉转移到腿上，我就去掐腿。别说，虽然眼泪疯狂流，但是不眨眼了。
都查完回家等结果。刚刚看甲亢是没有的，哼，嫉妒我眼睛大！ 干眼症周一再去看看吧。
20250804，我又去医院了，去的时候我心想，今天必须有个说法了。我可不想是那种工作病，工作病就是那种，一上班就不舒服，不上班就没事。之前听好多人有过，上班的时候腿疼啊，头疼啊。一到周末就去看病，怎么也查不出来是什么病。这个班不上了，或者换个环境了，病好了！ 早上8点多我就到了，医生拿着我的干眼症检查报告，说，你这个睑腺（好像是说的这个）好少，然后说这个会产生油，保护眼睛，防止干，你这个相当于产生的的油太浑浊了，类似于地沟油。“ 地沟油？你才地沟油呢！医生说，多用热毛巾敷眼睛。我可怜的眼睛啊！ 我天生不上做科研的，油分泌不出来，为人太清爽了，不油腻。 我让医生给我看了甲功那个检测，医生说我眼睛有点凸，但是这个和度数高有关系。没有甲亢。 我可太高兴了。 然后医生让我定期来检查眼底。
回家的路上，看看外面的树和阳光，我要好好对你，我的眼睛！ 看眼睛这个事也算是告一段落了！ 下一个会是什么病呢？哈哈哈哈哈哈！
